# Coming from gt {#chp:gt}

If you know [**gt**](https://gt.rstudio.com), you already know most of **lt**.
This chapter is a travel guide for crossing the border: a phrasebook (which
`lt_*()` function says what the `gt` function said), a list of the places where
the local customs differ, and a few souvenirs (a runnable example and a recipe
for static HTML).

We deeply appreciate **gt**'s pioneering work. It set the standard for display
tables in R, and **lt** owes much of its design vocabulary---headers, spanners,
row groups, footnotes---to the ground **gt** broke. **lt** is not a criticism of
**gt**; it is a different point on the trade-off curve. **lt** targets HTML
output only, and in exchange keeps its dependencies and its runtime tiny.[^gt-html]

[^gt-html]: HTML-first does not mean HTML-only for your final artifacts.
    `lt_export()` renders a table to PDF or PNG (via a headless browser) as well
    as to static HTML, so you can still drop an **lt** table into a paper or
    slide deck. It just builds those from the HTML rather than from a separate
    rendering backend (see @chp:export).

::: {.callout-tip data-legend="gt > < lt"}
A happy coincidence fits the spirit of this trade-off: in the comparison
operators **gt** is *greater than* and **lt** is *less than*. **lt** does
deliberately less.
:::

How much less? **gt** pulls in about 54 recursive dependencies (base64enc, cli,
dplyr, htmltools, V8, ...), whereas **lt** depends only on **xfun**. The output
is styled to look like **gt** by default, so in most cases you only need to
translate the function calls.

The mapping and the notes below distill the practical experience of three real
migrations, and you can read their pull requests for more worked examples:

-   [Merck/gsDesign2#629](https://github.com/Merck/gsDesign2/pull/629)
-   [keaven/gsDesign#282](https://github.com/keaven/gsDesign/pull/282)
-   [keaven/gsDesignNB#48](https://github.com/keaven/gsDesignNB/pull/48)

## The phrasebook {#sec:mapping}

Nearly every `lt_*()` function has a **gt** counterpart. The tables below cover
the common ones, grouped by what you are trying to say; the last table lists
things **lt** can do that have no direct **gt** equivalent.

### Building the table

| gt | lt |
|------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------|
| `gt(x)` | `lt(x)` |
| `gt(x, groupname_col = "col")` (separator rows) | `lt(x) \|> lt_group(~ col, sep = TRUE)` |
| `gt(x, groupname_col = "col", row_group_as_column = TRUE)` | `lt(x) \|> lt_group(~ col, sep = FALSE)` (rowspan) |
| `dplyr::group_by(x, col) \|> gt()` | `dplyr::group_by(x, col) \|> lt()` |

### Labels, headers, spanners, and notes

| gt | lt |
|------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------|
| `tab_header(title=, subtitle=)` | `lt_header(title=, subtitle=)` |
| `tab_spanner(label=, columns=)` | `lt_spanner(label=, columns=)` |
| `cols_label(a = "A")` | `lt_label(a = "A")` |
| `tab_footnote(footnote, cells_title("title"))` | `lt_footnote(text, "title")` |
| `tab_footnote(footnote, cells_title("subtitle"))` | `lt_footnote(text, "subtitle")` |
| `tab_footnote(footnote, cells_column_labels(col))` | `lt_footnote(text, "column", columns)` |
| `tab_footnote(footnote, cells_column_spanners(sp))` | `lt_footnote(text, "spanner", columns)` |
| `tab_footnote(footnote, cells_row_groups(grp))` | `lt_footnote(text, "group", columns, match=)` |
| `tab_footnote(footnote, cells_body(col, rows))` | `lt_footnote(text, "body", columns, rows)` |
| `tab_footnote(footnote)` (no location) | `lt_note(text)` |
| `tab_source_note(source_note=)` | `lt_note(text)` |

### Formatting values

| gt | lt |
|------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------|
| `fmt_number(columns=, decimals=)` | `lt_format(columns, decimals=)` |
| `fmt_percent(columns=)` | `lt_format(columns, percent = TRUE)` |
| `fmt_date(columns=)` | `lt_date(columns)` |
| `sub_missing()` / `sub_zero()` / `sub_small_vals()` | `lt_sub(missing=, zero=, small=)` |
| `html(value)` (mark a value as raw HTML) | `I(value)` (title/labels/footnotes); `lt_html(columns)` for body cells |
| `fmt_*()` applied to everything, by hand | automatic: `lt(auto_format = TRUE)` (@sec:auto) |

### Layout and styling

| gt | lt |
|------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------|
| `cols_align(align=, columns=)` | `lt_align(columns, align=)` |
| `cols_width(col ~ px(100))` | `lt_width(col = "100px")` |
| `cols_move(columns=, after=)` / `cols_move_to_start()` | `lt_move(columns, after=)` |
| `cols_merge(columns=, pattern=)` | `lt_merge(columns, pattern=)` |
| `cols_hide(columns)` | `lt_hide(columns)` |
| `tab_stub_indent(rows=, indent=)` | `lt_indent(rows, level=)` |
| `tab_style(style=, locations=)` | `lt_style(columns=, rows=, ...)` |
| `opt_css(css=)` | `lt_css(...)` |

### Interactivity

**gt** splits interactivity across `opt_interactive()` and `cols_hide()`; **lt**
gathers it all into `lt_interactive()`.

| gt | lt |
|------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------|
| `opt_interactive(use_sorting=, use_search=)` | `lt_interactive(sort=, search=)` |
| `opt_interactive(use_filters = TRUE)` | `lt_interactive(filter = TRUE)` (or `"auto"`, the default) |
| `opt_interactive(use_pagination=, page_size_default = n)` | `lt_interactive(pager = c(n, ...))` |
| `opt_interactive(use_resizers = TRUE)` | `lt_interactive(resize = TRUE)` (the default) |
| `cols_hide(columns)` (always hidden) | `lt_hide(columns)` |
| --- (reader toggles columns) | `lt_interactive(hide=)` (a column menu) |

### Output and Shiny

| gt                    | lt                                  |
|-----------------------|-------------------------------------|
| `gtsave(x, file)`     | `lt_export(x, file)`                |
| `gt_output()` (Shiny) | `lt_output()`                       |
| `render_gt()` (Shiny) | `render_lt()`                       |

### Things gt does not do (or needs an add-on for)

Some of **lt**'s verbs have no **gt** twin, and a few overlap with what you might
have used **DT** or **gtExtras** for.

| You want ... | In lt | Chapter |
|------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------|---------------|
| A forest plot or confidence intervals in cells | `lt_errorbar()` | @chp:plots |
| Sparklines (lines or bars) in cells | `lt_sparkline()` (cf. **gtExtras**) | @chp:plots |
| Before/after dots on a shared scale | `lt_dotplot()` | @chp:plots |
| Column types under the labels | `lt(show_types = TRUE)` | @sec:types |
| A search box that understands `price over 100, color is red or blue` | `lt_interactive(search = )` | @chp:interactive |
| Per-column filters picked from the data (sliders, checklists) | `lt_interactive(filter = "auto")` | @chp:interactive |
| A mini histogram of each column | `lt_interactive(profile = TRUE)` | @chp:interactive |
| Expandable row detail | `lt_interactive(detail = )` | @chp:interactive |
| Download the filtered view as CSV | `lt_interactive(download = )` | @chp:interactive |
| A one-call data explorer | `lt_viewer(x)` | @sec:viewer |
| Millions of rows (rows stay in R, pages are fetched) | `lt_serve()` (cf. **DT**'s server-side processing) | @chp:interactive |
| An editable table as a Shiny input | `lt_input()` / `lt_update()` (cf. **DT**'s `editable`) | @chp:shiny |
| The table as plain JSON, to embed elsewhere | `lt_spec()` / `lt_dependency()` | @chp:export |

## Notable differences {#sec:differences}

A few places where **lt** works differently enough from **gt** to be worth
spelling out, drawn from porting **gsDesign2**, **gsDesign**, and **gsDesignNB**.
None of them is hard, but each is the kind of thing you only learn by tripping
over it once, so consider this the cheaper way.

### Column selection: strings or positions, not tidy-select {#sec:selection}

**gt** uses tidy-select, so unquoted column names and `tidyselect` helpers work.
**lt** deliberately does not: it takes column names as *character strings* (or
integer positions, or a one-sided formula). Tidy-select's ergonomic win is
mostly at the console. The cost is a large conceptual surface (data masking,
quosures, injection) and painful programmatic use: the moment a column name comes
from a variable, you are into `{{ }}` and `all_of()` machinery. For a package
whose calls are often generated from code, plain strings win, so that is what
**lt** takes.

```r
# gt
tab_spanner(label = "Bounds", columns = c(alt, null))
# lt
lt_spanner(label = "Bounds", columns = c("alt", "null"))   # quote them
lt_spanner(label = "Bounds", columns = c(4, 5))            # or use positions
lt_spanner(Bounds ~ alt + null)                            # or a (compact) formula
```

If you dislike quoting names, the formula interface keeps them bare:
`Bounds ~ alt + null` puts the label on the left and the columns on the right,
the same as `label = "Bounds", columns = c("alt", "null")`. It relies only on base
R's formula, with no non-standard evaluation machinery: the names stay
unevaluated symbols you can read off directly. Non-syntactic names work too,
quoted in backticks: `` Bounds ~ `Alternate hypothesis` + `Null hypothesis` ``.

The formula also does duty for tidy-select *predicates*. In `lt_format()`,
`lt_align()`, and friends, a **one-sided** formula whose right side is a logical
expression selects the columns for which it is `TRUE`, with `.` bound to the
vector of column names. So **gt**'s "all columns but one" idiom translates
cleanly:

```r
# gt: format every numeric column
fmt_number(columns = where(is.numeric), decimals = 4)
# lt: select by name, not by type
lt_format(~ . != "Metric", decimals = 4)   # every column except Metric
```

::: {.callout-warning data-legend="Names, not types"}
Note what is being tested. `where(is.numeric)` inspects each column's *values*
(its type), whereas the **lt** formula sees only the column *names* in `.`. There
is no name-based way to say "the numeric ones", so pick out the columns you do
*not* want to format by name (often the single label column) and negate, or list
the ones you do. (Tables already format numeric columns on their own, so you may
not need `lt_format()` at all; see @sec:auto.)
:::

### Interactivity is one function, not a separate step {#sec:one-interactive}

**gt** turns on client-side interactivity with `opt_interactive()`, and hides
columns with the unrelated `cols_hide()`. **lt** folds all of it into
`lt_interactive()`: sorting, searching, filtering, paging, resizing, row detail,
profiles, a CSV download, and a reader-togglable column menu. Whatever you do not
ask for is not loaded, so non-interactive tables cost nothing extra
(@chp:interactive).

### Footnotes and source notes are two different functions {#sec:footnotes-vs-notes}

`gt::tab_footnote()` does double duty: with a location it attaches a footnote to
cells; without one it adds a general note. **lt** splits these:

-   `lt_footnote(text, where, columns, rows, match)` attaches a footnote to a
    location and gives it a marker. `text` is the *first* positional argument
    (not the location). `where` is one of `"title"`, `"subtitle"`, `"column"`,
    `"spanner"`, `"group"`, `"body"`. For `"column"` and `"spanner"` pass the
    name(s) in `columns`; for `"body"` also pass `rows`; for `"group"` you can use
    `match = "starts_with"` to match a group label by prefix.
-   `lt_note(text)` adds a plain table note at the bottom. It is also the
    replacement for `tab_source_note()`.

### Row groups: `lt_group(~ col)`, and two rendering styles {#sec:groups}

**gt** groups either via `gt(groupname_col=)` or a preceding
`dplyr::group_by()`. In **lt**, grouping is a separate step, `lt_group(~ col)`,
with a one-sided formula for the grouping column.

There are two rendering styles, chosen by `sep`:

-   **Separator rows**: the group label sits on its own full-width row above the
    group. This is **gt**'s default; in **lt** you request it with `sep = TRUE`.
-   **Rowspan**: the group value is a merged cell down the left. This is
    **gt**'s `row_group_as_column = TRUE`; in **lt** you request it with
    `sep = FALSE`.

**lt**'s default is neither: `sep = "auto"` picks rowspan for short labels and
separator rows once any label exceeds about 20 characters. So a **gt** table
will not necessarily match out of the box. Set `sep` explicitly if you need a
specific style.

```r
# gt default (separator rows)
x |> group_by(Analysis) |> gt()
# lt equivalent
lt(x) |> lt_group(~ Analysis, sep = TRUE)
```

You can also group by more than one column, `lt_group(~ a + b)`, which nests the
groups as rowspan cells (`a` spanning `b`). Separator rows work for a single
column only, so multi-column grouping always renders as rowspan. This is a real
difference from **gt**, which has only one level of row groups: `groupname_col`
takes a single column, and multiple grouping variables are flattened into one
combined label (joined by `row_group.sep`, default `" - "`) rather than nested.

**Groups from row conditions, and controlling their order.** **gt** can define
groups on the fly from row predicates (a `tab_row_group(label=, rows=<cond>)` per
group) and then set their order with `row_group_order()`. **lt** has no predicate
form: it groups only by the value of an existing column. So the port is to
*materialize that column first*. Build a factor whose levels are the group order
you want (e.g., with `data.table::fcase()` or nested `ifelse()`), sort the data
by it, and group on it with `sort = FALSE` so that **lt** keeps your row order
instead of re-sorting the labels alphabetically:

```r
# gt: groups defined by conditions, ordered explicitly
tab_row_group(label = "Power",  rows = Metric == "Power") |>
tab_row_group(label = "Events", rows = grepl("Events", Metric)) |>
row_group_order(groups = c("Events", "Power"))

# lt: derive an ordered factor column, then group by it
df$Group = factor(
  ifelse(grepl("Events", df$Metric), "Events", "Power"),
  levels = c("Events", "Power")          # desired group order
)
df = df[order(df$Group), ]
lt(df) |> lt_group(~ Group, sep = TRUE, sort = FALSE)
```

`sort = FALSE` is the key. By default `lt_group()` sorts rows by the grouping
value, which would discard the factor order you set. With it off, the groups
appear in first-seen row order, i.e., the factor-level order you sorted into.

::: {.callout-tip data-legend="Smaller escape hatches"}
If all you need is to reorder groups that already exist, you do not need a factor:
a second `lt_group()` call with the labels in the order you want does it, and
`lt_group("Label" = rows)` defines groups by hand from row numbers
(@sec:group-manual).
:::

### Raw HTML: `I()` is the new `html()` and `md()` {#sec:raw-html}

To keep raw HTML (e.g., a line break) from being escaped in a title, column
label, or footnote, wrap it in `I()`:

```r
lt_label(theta = I("Underlying<br>response rate"))
```

`I()` is also the answer to **gt**'s `md()`. **gt** lets you wrap a title or label
in `md("**bold**")` to render Markdown; **lt** has no Markdown-in-labels
equivalent. Pass plain text (the common case: `md("**Power**")` simply becomes
`"Power"`), or, if you truly need formatting, use `I()` with raw HTML:
`I("<b>Power</b>")`. For body cells, mark whole columns with `lt_html()`
(@sec:html).

### Substitutions: the defaults already do the work {#sec:sub-defaults}

Two `lt_sub()` defaults are worth knowing before you translate a `sub_*()` call.
Missing values already render as an em dash (`—`), and nothing special is done to
zeros or small values. So a `sub_missing(missing_text = "—")` in **gt** is
usually just noise in **lt**: drop it unless you want a *different* placeholder.

### Styling: you probably don't need CSS {#sec:styling}

**lt**'s default look is close to **gt**'s out of the box, so you rarely need CSS
just to reproduce **gt**'s base appearance. The whole stylesheet
([`lt.min.css`](https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@xiee/utils/css/lt.min.css)) is only
a couple of kilobytes, and it is deliberately unopinionated: it sets borders,
spacing, and alignment, but does *not* impose a `font-family` or a table-wide
`font-size` (only the title and subtitle get relative sizes). It inherits the
surrounding page's typography instead.

Because it declares so little, you can override or extend it with a few plain CSS
rules, with no need to fight a heavy default. Add them with `lt_css()` and
`lt_style()` (@chp:style), or just drop a `<style>` element or a chunk into your
document, e.g.:

```css
.lt-table { font-size: 0.9em; width: 100%; }
```

## Generating a static HTML table {#sec:gt-static}

By default an **lt** table is built in the browser by the JavaScript runtime
(@chp:js) at view time, which is perfect for HTML pages but useless for output
that must already contain the finished `<table>`: a GitHub `README.md`, an email,
a cached page. `lt_export(x, file)` bakes the table into static HTML instead,
running the runtime once at export time (it can also write images and other
formats, depending on the file extension). Because it runs the runtime, baking
needs a JavaScript engine: either Node.js or a headless browser (e.g.,
Chrome, Chromium, or Edge).[^gt-v8]

[^gt-v8]: This does *not* undercut **lt**'s lightweight promise. The engine is an
    *opt-in runtime* tool, not an install dependency: installing **lt** still
    pulls in only **xfun**. You need Node or a browser only on the occasional
    static-export path. The common cases (HTML pages, Shiny, litedown, pkgdown)
    render client-side in the browser the reader already has, needing nothing
    extra. And a headless browser is present on nearly every machine, while Node
    is a cheap, pure-tooling install. Contrast **gt**, which pulls in the V8
    JavaScript engine unconditionally at install time (via **juicyjuice**, a plain
    `Imports`), and for a different purpose: **gt** builds the table in R and uses
    V8 to *inline its CSS* into per-element `style=` attributes. **lt** needs no
    such step. It links or embeds its tiny stylesheet (or omits it with
    `css = FALSE`). Keeping the styles in a stylesheet is also easier to
    customize: inline `style=` attributes carry high specificity, so a reader's
    own stylesheet cannot override them without `!important` or editing the
    markup, whereas an ordinary rule can restyle an **lt** table freely.
    (Inlining is genuinely useful for email, where `<style>` blocks are often
    stripped. It is the right tool there, just not a good default elsewhere.)

Inside R Markdown you do not need to call `lt_export()` per table: set
`options(lt.lt_static = list(...))` and every `lt()` chunk in the document is
baked with those arguments automatically. *This option only takes effect when
knitting an Rmd*; anywhere else it does nothing, and you must call
`lt_export()` explicitly.

That option is how **gsDesign2** turns `README.Rmd` into a `README.md` that GitHub
renders with real tables. The trick is a custom `knit` field in the YAML header:
it enables static baking, then knits directly with `knitr::knit()` instead of
going through Pandoc. Pandoc would otherwise reformat the baked table, inserting
extra blank lines inside it; GitHub then reads those blanks as paragraph breaks
and wraps each cell's content in a `<p>`, adding ugly large margins inside every
cell.

```yaml
---
# Use knitr::knit() directly to avoid pandoc reformatting raw HTML tables.
knit: |
  (function(inputFile, encoding) {
    options(lt.lt_static = list(fragment = TRUE, css = FALSE))
    output = knitr::knit(inputFile, encoding = encoding)
    body = xfun::yaml_body(xfun::read_utf8(output), parse = FALSE)$body
    body = body[cumsum(nzchar(body)) > 0]
    xfun::write_utf8(body, output)
  })
---
```

With that header, each `lt(data)` chunk in the README emits a finished `<table>`
straight into `README.md`, with no post-processing needed.

## A runnable example {#sec:demo}

Here is a small table that exercises most of the mappings above. Each comment
names the **gt** function that would have done the job:

```{r demo}
df = data.frame(
  grp  = c("A", "A", "B", "B"),
  item = c("x", "y", "x", "y"),
  lo   = c(0.1234, 0.3401, 0.2087, 0.4523),
  hi   = c(0.8812, 0.6644, 0.7912, 0.5498)
)

lt(df) |>
  lt_group(~ grp, sep = TRUE) |>                       # gt: groupname_col
  lt_label(item = "Item", lo = "Lower", hi = "Upper") |>  # gt: cols_label
  lt_spanner(Probability ~ lo + hi) |>                 # gt: tab_spanner
  lt_format(~ lo + hi, decimals = 2) |>                # gt: fmt_number
  lt_header(title = "Demo", subtitle = "gt -> lt") |>  # gt: tab_header
  lt_footnote("Interval bounds.", "spanner", "Probability") |>  # tab_footnote
  lt_note("Source: synthetic data.")                   # gt: tab_source_note
```

If your own package builds **gt** tables for its result classes, the next chapter
shows how to offer **lt** tables the idiomatic way: with an S3 method for `lt()`
(@chp:extend).
